human_tolerance.notes: Finds fruit and insects in gardens and leftovers in municipal waste easily available, and sleeps in hollows in old garden trees, cottages, garages, abandoned houses and attics. Individuals range only 3 to 40 hectares in small towns and suburbs, so it lives right alongside people, but it keeps to den sites and cover and slips away rather than confronting.

phases.name: mating
phases.note: Mating is triggered by increasing daylight between late January and mid-March, with large regional differences: southern states mate later than average, and in Manitoba the season peaks in March and runs to June. Males roam their home ranges looking for females during the three to four days when conception is possible.

phases.name: young
phases.note: After 63 to 65 days of gestation a litter of typically two to five kits is born in spring, blind and deaf at about 10 cm long and 60-75 g; they begin to leave the den at about 1 kg, take solid food at six to nine weeks, are weaned by 16 weeks, and are shown dens and feeding grounds before splitting up in the fall.

phases.name: territorial
phases.note: Raccoons stay active through the winter in tree hollows, rock crevices and other sheltered dens rather than hibernating, and can lose as much as half their body weight to fat reserves before spring.

vocalizations.description: The birdlike twittering of newborn kits, one of thirteen identified vocal calls of which seven are used between a mother and her kits.

taxonomy.note: Procyonidae, Procyon, (Linnaeus, 1758); Procyon is derived from a Greek word used by the Greeks for a similar animal, and lotor is Latin for washer.

external.note: GBIF usage key 5218786 and iNaturalist taxon 41663; ITIS TSN 9654 from Wikidata P685.

common_names.note: Called the raccoon, the North American, northern or common raccoon to distinguish it from other raccoon species.

conservation.note: Native to and widespread in North America with no threat described, consistent with Least Concern in its native range; no IUCN page was consulted because those are not openly licensed. Its status elsewhere is different: it is on the EU list of Invasive Alien Species of Union Concern since 2016.

range.note: Native to North America, with the eastern raccoon occurring in all US states and Canadian provinces north of South Carolina and Tennessee and island subspecies in the Caribbean and Central America. Escapes and deliberate introductions in the mid-20th century put it in central Europe, the Caucasus and Japan.

traits.locomotion_modes.note: Plantigrade locomotion, top speed 16 to 24 km/h over short distances, and it can swim at an average of about 5 km/h and stay in the water for several hours. Climb is left out of locomotion_modes because the quadruped body plan has no climb pose to draw, though raccoons do climb trees to escape threats.

traits.nest_type.note: Cavity: 'Tree hollows in old oaks or other trees and rock crevices are preferred by raccoons as sleeping, winter, and litter dens', with burrows dug by other mammals, dense undergrowth or tree crotches used when hollows are unavailable.

traits.perching.note: It climbs to escape but rests and sleeps in dens rather than perching, so it is not treated as perching.

traits.size_class.note: From mass_kg: about 8 kg is under 50 kg, so Medium.

traits.mass_kg.note: Body weight can range from 2 to 26 kg but is usually between 5 and 12 kg; 8 kg is the mid-point of the usual band.

traits.mass_range_kg.note: It can range from 2 to 26 kg, varying with habitat, with the largest wild raccoon recorded at 28.4 kg.

traits.length_m.note: Head to hindquarters 40 to 70 cm, not counting the bushy tail, which measures 20 to 40 cm but is usually not much longer than 25 cm; 55 cm is the mid-range body length.

traits.shoulder_height_m.note: The shoulder height is between 23 and 30 cm; 27 cm is the mid-range value.

traits.lifespan_y.note: 'The species' life expectancy in the wild is only 1.8 to 3.1 years, depending on the local conditions such as traffic volume, hunting, and weather severity'; 2.5 years is the mid-point. Captive raccoons live over 20 years.

traits.diet.note: 'It is usually nocturnal and omnivorous, eating about 40% invertebrates, 33% plants, and 27% vertebrates.' The plant third is split into fruit and browse, and the vertebrate share includes amphibians, crustaceans and other animals taken around water.

traits.social.note: Related females share a common area in a fission-fusion society and unrelated males form loose social groups that usually do not consist of more than four individuals.

traits.activity_pattern.note: 'It is usually nocturnal', with healthy animals, especially nursing mothers, occasionally foraging during the day.

traits.defense.note: Raccoons avoid open terrain, depend on vertical structures to climb when threatened, and slip away to a den; they do not confront people.

traits.wariness.note: Judgement, set from its use of urban dens and human food sources against its dependence on den sites and cover; it is confident around people but keeps to escape routes.

habitat.use.note: Original habitat of deciduous and mixed forest, now including mountainous areas, coastal marshes and urban areas; it forages on the ground and on lowland shores and climbs trees when threatened.

habitat.shelter_tag.note: Tree hollows and rock crevices preferred for sleeping, winter and litter dens.

habitat.resources.note: The diet percentages give the invertebrate, small_vertebrate, fruit and browse weights; cavity and burrow from the den line, and water from its swimming and shoreline dabbling. Weights are authored to match the diet shares.

habitat.human_tolerance.note: Present in metropolitan areas since the 1950s, with urban home ranges of only 3 to 40 hectares for females; 'Fruit and insects in gardens and leftovers in municipal waste are easily available food sources', and urban sleeping places include hollows in old garden trees, cottages, garages, abandoned houses and attics.

seasonal.strategy.note: Raccoons use winter dens but the article describes no hibernation, and it reports a winter weight loss driven by fat reserves rather than dormancy, so the animal is treated as active year-round.

seasonal.phases.note: Mating between late January and mid-March, triggered by increasing daylight; 63 to 65 days of gestation; a litter of typically two to five kits born in spring; solid food at six to nine weeks, weaned by 16 weeks; and the juvenile group splitting up in the fall after the mother has shown them dens and feeding grounds.

seasonal.life_stages.note: Kits are usually weaned by 16 weeks, taken as 112 days; scale is an authored juvenile size, and the birth weight of 60-75 g is far smaller than the model's smallest form.

vocalizations.twitter.note: Seven of thirteen identified vocal calls are used in communication between a mother and her kits, one of these being the birdlike twittering of newborns.

look.note: Greyish coat of dense underfur with long stiff guard hairs shaded in grey and, to a lesser extent, brown; black fur around the eyes contrasting sharply with the surrounding white face colouring; slightly rounded ears bordered by white fur; and alternating light and dark rings on the tail. Proportions are authored.

behavior.note: The shared ground-forager program fits a nocturnal omnivore that forages over a small home range, drinks and dabbles at water, retreats to a den to sleep through the day and bolts for cover when threatened. The rest-sun window is set around daylight because the animal is nocturnal. Parameters are authored.
